purpose: Mexiletine is used to treat certain types of irregular heartbeats, called arrhythmias, to help your heart beat in a steady, normal rhythm. It is also sometimes used off-label to help relieve certain types of nerve pain or muscle stiffness. Your doctor prescribed it to help keep your heart rhythm under control and reduce symptoms like palpitations or dizziness.
how_it_works: Your heart uses electrical signals to beat in a regular pattern. Mexiletine works by calming down overactive electrical signals in the heart muscle that can cause it to beat too fast or irregularly. Think of it like a dimmer switch that turns down the electrical activity just enough to keep your heart beating smoothly and steadily.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, or upset stomach are the most common side effects, especially when you first start taking it. You might also notice dizziness, shakiness or tremor, heartburn, or feeling lightheaded. Taking it with food or milk can help reduce stomach upset.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you notice your heartbeat feeling worse, very fast, or very slow. This medicine can rarely make arrhythmias worse in some people. Let your doctor know if you have liver problems, a history of heart failure, or low blood pressure. Do not stop taking this medication suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this could be dangerous. Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol and always tell all your doctors and pharmacist about every medication you take, including over-the-counter drugs, since many medications can interact with mexiletine.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 200 mg taken by mouth every 8 hours (three times a day) with food or milk to protect your stomach. Your doctor may slowly adjust your dose based on how well it works and how you tolerate it. The maximum dose is generally 1,200 mg per day. Always take it exactly as your doctor tells you and do not skip doses.
